posts.headline: DevOps & Cloud Engineer | • Networking • AWS • Kubernetes • Docker •Terraform • CI/CD • Jenkins | Helping students & freshers build strong tech careers | BCA CSE (Cloud Technology)
posts.text: The biggest shift I’ve seen in the DevOps market this year: Companies are done hiring “tool operators”. They want people who can: - Design reliable systems - Reduce incident frequency - Make infrastructure cheaper and safer - Enable developers to ship faster without breaking things That’s why pure “DevOps Engineer” roles are shrinking and specialized roles are growing. High-demand skills right now: → Production-grade Kubernetes → Infrastructure as Code (Terraform / Pulumi) → GitOps (ArgoCD / Flux) → Observability + SLOs → Cloud architecture (AWS/Azure/GCP deep, not surface level) → Automation + Python → Basic security mindset (DevSecOps) Entry-level is extremely competitive. Mid-level people with real ownership and measurable impact are still landing good roles. Stop chasing every new tool. Start solving real problems. How’s the job market treating you in 2026? Drop your experience below. #DevOps #PlatformEngineering #SRE #CloudJobs #CareerAdvice

posts.text: 𝐈𝐬 𝐀𝐈 𝐦𝐚𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐮𝐬 𝐟𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐫 — 𝐨𝐫 𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭 𝐥𝐚𝐳𝐲 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐬𝐭𝐮𝐩𝐢𝐝? AI slop ruined software engineering. And I say that as someone who learned to code in the GPT era. My phone died in May. Full reset. 7 months of expense data, gone. My first instinct? Dump my bank statements into an AI model and get a clean CSV back. Then I stopped. My entire financial life, handed to a cloud model, to do date parsing. Like hiring a Michelin chef to boil water. I tried a local model instead. Qwen3 4B. Too dumb. Couldn't even read the locked PDF. Then I found a 2010 Reddit post. Some guy with the exact same problem. He wrote a parser. A few hundred lines. Ran in milliseconds, touched no network. Still works today. That's when I finally understood the hate old engineers have for AI slop. Not bitterness — mourning. They watched a generation skip learning how machines actually work. Wrote the full story on my blog: https://lnkd.in/dhNS6XBs #SoftwareEngineering #BuildInPublic

posts.author: Shivangi Tiwari
posts.headline: Growth & Brand Marketing Leader | Ex-Software Engineer | Founder, Brandinia | Tech & Career Creator (400K+)
posts.text: The tech industry says it can't find talent. But is it willing to build talent? Think about the contradiction: → Freshers need experience to get hired. → Experienced engineers are getting laid off. → Developers are expected to master new tools while doing more with less. Yet companies still struggle to find the “right talent.” And the data makes this more interesting: → LinkedIn's 2026 US hiring data shows entry-level hiring down 6% year over year. → A 2026 IZA research paper found junior software developer vacancies declined 14–15% relative to senior vacancies following ChatGPT's release. The problem isn't just a shortage of talent. It's also how companies hire and develop it. You can't keep raising the bar for entry-level roles while removing the opportunities people need to reach that bar. For developers, now just learning another framework wouldn't help . It's building fundamentals, solving real problems, and learning to use AI without outsourcing your judgment, etc etc! What's your take? Are we facing a talent shortage or a willingness-to-train shortage?

posts.text: 𝗙𝗗𝗘: 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗠𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗩𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗧𝗲𝗰𝗵 𝗥𝗼𝗹𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗔𝗜 𝗘𝗿𝗮? There’s a term creating a massive shift across the global IT industry right now: Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE). 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗲𝘅𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗹𝘆 𝗶𝘀 𝗮𝗻 𝗙𝗗𝗘? In simple terms, traditional Software Engineers are usually handed a clear blueprint and told what to build. An FDE, on the other hand, sits directly with the client. They immerse themselves in the business context, uncover the root problems, and independently design and execute end-to-end solutions using Software, AI, Automation, and Data. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗣𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗙𝗗𝗘 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹: 𝗔 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗦𝘁𝘂𝗱𝘆 This model was pioneered by Palantir. After the conflict in Ukraine, an estimated 𝟭𝟱𝟲,𝟬𝟬𝟬 𝘀𝗾𝘂𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗸𝗶𝗹𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀 of land were contaminated with landmines. Using traditional detection methods, clearing the region would have taken nearly 𝟳𝟱𝟳 𝘆𝗲𝗮𝗿𝘀. Palantir’s Forward Deployed Engineers stepped in. Working alongside government officials on-site, they integrated over 100 disparate datasets—mapping road networks, agricultural fields, power lines, and hospitals—to algorithmically prioritize clearance efforts. The result? Instead of centuries, 𝟴𝟬% 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗶𝘀 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝗯𝗲 𝘀𝗮𝗳𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘂𝘀𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝟭𝟬 𝘆𝗲𝗮𝗿𝘀. That is the essence of an FDE: They don't just write code off a spec sheet; they solve critical real-world problems. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗜𝗻𝗱𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘆 𝗣𝗮𝗿𝗮𝗱𝗶𝗴𝗺 𝗦𝗵𝗶𝗳𝘁 While IT giants are scaling back traditional entry-level positions and low-complexity support roles due to AI automation, frontier tech companies like 𝗢𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗔𝗜, 𝗚𝗼𝗼𝗴𝗹𝗲, 𝗔𝗻𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗼𝗽𝗶𝗰, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗣𝗮𝗹𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗿 are aggressively hiring FDEs. Top-tier FDEs are currently commanding salaries 𝟲 𝘁𝗼 𝟳 𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲𝘀 𝗵𝗶𝗴𝗵𝗲𝗿 than conventional software engineers. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗧𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗮𝘄𝗮𝘆 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗦𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗵 𝗔𝘀𝗶𝗮𝗻 𝗜𝗧 & 𝗦𝘂𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗳𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹𝘀 For professionals relying on legacy manual workflows—such as routine customer support, manual troubleshooting, data entry, or repetitive testing—the signal is clear: 𝗔𝗜 𝗶𝘀 𝗮𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘀𝗲 𝗳𝘂𝗻𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝘁 𝗮𝗻 𝘂𝗻𝗽𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗲𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗽𝗮𝗰𝗲. The rule of the new AI economy is simple:. 𝗦𝘁𝗼𝗽 𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗺𝗮𝗻𝘂𝗮𝗹 𝗹𝗮𝗯𝗼𝗿. 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝗹𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗵𝗶𝗴𝗵-𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗲 𝘀𝗼𝗹𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀. To future-proof your career, the focus must urgently shift toward 𝗔𝗜 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗴𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻, 𝗖𝗹𝗼𝘂𝗱 𝗜𝗻𝗳𝗿𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲, 𝗔𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝗶𝗰 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺-𝗦𝗼𝗹𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴.

posts.text: 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝗳 𝗔𝗜 𝗺𝗮𝗱𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝘁𝗲𝗮𝗺 𝟯× 𝗯𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗲𝗿 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝘁 𝟯× 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲? A study of 500,000+ GitHub developers found something fascinating. Autonomous coding agents were associated with a 𝟮𝟰𝟬% 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗶𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗶𝘁𝘆, 𝗯𝘂𝘁 𝗼𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝗮 𝟯𝟬% 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗶𝗻 𝘀𝗼𝗳𝘁𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘀, according to the study's estimates. More commits. More code. More activity. But a much smaller increase in what actually ships. It's like hiring 10 chefs who prep ingredients at lightning speed, only to discover your kitchen has one oven. 😂 As a full-stack engineer, I see a version of this in my own work. Generating code is the fast part now. Reviewing it, testing it, and making sure it fits the rest of the system is where the time goes. Anthropic's experience points to the same thing. Its engineering blog revealed that daily merged code changes grew from around 𝟮,𝟱𝟬𝟬 𝗶𝗻 𝗠𝗮𝘆 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲 to over 𝟯𝟬,𝟬𝟬𝟬 𝗶𝗻 𝗦𝗲𝗽𝘁𝗲𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗿. Anthropic responded by building its own version control system to handle its engineering needs. The bottleneck didn't disappear. It moved downstream. 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗵𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗻𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗲 𝗴𝗲𝘁𝘀 𝗳𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝘁? AI can generate another feature in minutes. Making sure it integrates, works reliably, and is worth shipping is a different challenge. Maybe the next AI productivity race isn't about who generates the most code. It's about who can turn that output into reliable software. 𝗕𝗲𝗰𝗮𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝗮 𝗯𝘂𝘀𝘆 𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗶𝘀𝗻'𝘁 𝗻𝗲𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗹𝘆 𝗮 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗼𝗻𝗲. 😉 #AI #SoftwareEngineering

posts.author: Chatresh Consultants
posts.text: A common topic in technical hiring syncs: why is evaluating junior engineering candidates becoming more difficult, even as applicant volumes soar? With AI-assisted code generators and hundreds of identical online tutorials, nearly every early-career portfolio looks functional on the surface. Hiring managers are routinely reviewing candidates with 4–5 projects that compile cleanly, yet finding that very few can discuss how their system actually operates under production conditions. When evaluating junior software developers, code volume is no longer a reliable signal. Instead, engineering teams look for evidence of how a candidate thinks through practical engineering trade-offs. Four key dimensions separate a tutorial-follower from an engineer ready to contribute to commercial codebases: 1. Architectural Reasoning Over Stack Breadth Listing ten languages or libraries on a CV shows enthusiasm, but depth shows competence. Can the candidate articulate why they chose PostgreSQL over MongoDB for a specific data model? Can they explain the caching strategy they selected? The ability to justify technical choices is far more valuable than knowing another syntax variation. 2. Version Control Discipline Commit history reveals communication and workflow habits. A single squash commit titled “finished app” suggests isolated work. In contrast, feature branching, atomic commits, descriptive pull request notes, and structured code reviews show that an engineer understands how to work within an enterprise team. 3. Graceful Failure & Error Boundaries Anyone can write software that succeeds on the happy path. Real systems face dropped connections, third-party API rate limits, invalid payloads, and race conditions. Candidates who design graceful degradations and actionable error logging stand out immediately. 4. Clear Documentation & System Architecture A production-ready repository is not complete without context. Including an architecture diagram, local containerization instructions (such as Docker), and an honest section detailing known technical debt proves empathy for teammates who will read and maintain the code later. Bridging the gap between theoretical computing education and production engineering standards is essential for building sustainable technical teams. At Chatresh, this philosophy is what guided the development of our practical immersion initiative, LUYSK (Level Up Your Skills) in Sevenoaks—creating an environment where aspiring developers learn to build, debug, and review software using the exact practices required by commercial teams. For engineering managers, tech leads, and founders: what is the most reliable green flag you look for when assessing early-career technical portfolios? #SoftwareEngineering #TechLeadership #EngineeringManagement #TechHiring #DeveloperTalent #SystemDesign #CodeQuality #STEMUK

posts.text: For the first time in decades, the Grace Hopper Celebration has been canceled. Even during COVID, the community came together for a virtual event. It’s hard to imagine a fall without GHC. I first attended as a graduate student presenting my research. A few years later, as a junior engineer at Microsoft, I organized a panel on software engineering practices. That led to volunteering on the conference committees, eventually chairing the entire program and kicking off the conference keynote. Somewhere along the way, I even brought my six-month-old daughter to a multi-day planning meeting at the AnitaB.org headquarters! GHC has been a constant throughout my career, across five companies, career changes, motherhood, and everything in between. I’ve attended as a student, speaker, organizer, hiring manager, and mentor. More importantly, I’ve made lifelong friends, including two inspiring women I met at my very first GHC (shoutout Alyona and Jiayue )! I was looking forward to speaking this year with another dear friend I met through GHC Monalisa about how AI is changing our roles as builders and leaders. Instead, I’m feeling sad about the cancellation and grateful for the people and experiences this community has brought into my life. For those who were planning to attend, especially students and early-career folks in tech who identify as women, I’d love to pay it forward! I’ve opened 12 free, 25-minute speed mentoring conversations over the next three Fridays. Happy to talk careers, technology, navigating change, or whatever is on your mind. Book a time here: https://lnkd.in/gU8M6-rM I hope this isn’t the end of GHC. And whatever happens, I hope we find ways to keep this community going.

posts.text: Everyone says this AI hiring wave is a real shift. Looking at how many software houses are opening "AI/ML Engineer" roles with no AI product behind them yet, I think a chunk of it is the dot-com bubble again. In 1999, a company didn't need revenue to raise money. It needed ".com" in the name, and investors lined up anyway. Pets .com and Webvan both raised tens of millions on that logic before Nasdaq lost close to 78% of its value by 2002. Same move now. Three different letters. A software house doesn't need a shipped AI product to open 3-4 "AI Engineer" reqs this quarter. It needs "AI" on the services page to win the next client pitch. Ask what the actual project is, and half the time there isn't one. The hiring happened first. The use case is still "we'll figure it out." That's a company renting a label, not building a product. Here's the part that worries me more than the bubble itself. Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex already let one backend engineer do what used to take three. When the AI hype cools, a software house sitting on tools like that don to cut the junior AI/ML hires. It needs abudget review. A dot-com company could at least argue the internet was real and the business model was wrong. This time, the tools replacing the engineer and the engineer gett the exact same technology.

posts.text: Why fear for ai triggered lay offs? Drdd’s perspective ——————————-The Software Industry’s Post-AI Turbulence: A Survival Blueprint for Engineers and CorporationsZoho CEO Sridhar Vembu recently raised alarm bells across the tech sector. He noted that skyrocketing AI compute costs, combined with industry-wide economic turbulence, will make freezes on hiring and increments common. While Vembu plans to refrain from layoffs, many corporates won't.This raises two critical questions that we must answer to navigate this shift:1. What can a middle-aged software professional do to elongate their career in this environment?2. What must the software industry do to survive, pivot, and grow?Here is a strategic blueprint to address both challenges.1. The Middle-Aged Engineer’s Longevity PlaybookAt this stage in your career, trying to out-pace entry-level developers in raw AI-assisted coding speed is a losing battle. Instead, your value lies in wisdom, system architecture, and optimization.• Become the "AI Auditor": AI writes code fast, but it introduces subtle architectural flaws, edge cases, and hallucinations. A seasoned professional must shift their focus to applying intelligent overall checks—auditing AI output against macro business logic.• Prove Value with the Three-Tiered AI Pilot: When corporates slash programming consultant budgets, don't just argue your worth—prove it mathematically. Pit three project execution models against each other: 1. No-AI Execution vs. 2. Full-AI Execution vs. 3. Hybrid/Moderate AI BudgetPresent the exact metrics on cost, delivery time, and minimum error rates to corporate leadership. Show them exactly how you optimize their AI spend.• Focus on Traceable High-Yield Areas: Anchor your daily AI use in highly measurable zones like QA, automated testing, and CI/CD pipelines where productivity metrics are mathematically undeniable. posts.author: Mir Furqaan
posts.headline: -- GenAI Engineer & Data Analyst | Python | RAG | LLMs | SQL | Power BI | FastAPI | Machine Learning --
posts.text: Two headlines hit my feed today, and they don't agree with each other. Headline one: US software developer job postings are up nearly 𝟭𝟱% since February 2025 — the month AI coding tools went mainstream — while overall job postings fell about 7%. (Indeed Hiring Lab data, reported by CNBC.) Headline two: entry-level developer employment is down roughly 𝟮𝟬%, and AI-related employment for 22–25-year-olds fell 16%. (Stanford's 2026 AI Index.) Both are true. That contradiction is the whole story. Demand didn't vanish — it moved. The growth is in senior and 𝗔𝗜-𝘁𝗶𝘁𝗹𝗲𝗱 roles: people who can own complex systems, verify AI output, and make calls the models can't. Stack Overflow's 2026 survey says the quiet part out loud — almost two-thirds of developers now use AI coding tools daily, but fewer than 10% trust AI with important decisions. Someone still has to be the adult in the room. I read this as a fresher on the hunt, and my honest take: "writes code" is a commodity skill now. 𝗗𝗶𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴, 𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗳𝘆𝗶𝗻𝗴, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽𝗽𝗶𝗻𝗴 AI-assisted work is the scarce one. Case in point: when I built my DocMind AI RAG app, the model wrote a lot of the code. But it didn't design the chunking strategy, didn't build the citation system that made answers trustworthy, and didn't choose the embedding model or wire up auth. The judgment calls were the whole project. Three things that actually matter now: → Learn the tools AND the verification layer — code review, evaluation, audit trails. That's where the hiring moved. → Go deep on the unsexy architecture — API design, data pipelines, observability. AI writes functions; it doesn't design systems. → Build one project where YOU were the senior engineer — scoped it, evaluated it, defended the trade-offs. Interviews probe decisions, not keystrokes. And even if you never write code for a living — the same split is hitting every desk job: the tooling gets cheap, the judgment stays expensive. Which side of that split are you building for? #AICareers #SoftwareEngineering #TechJobs #GenerativeAI #Freshers

posts.text: The entry-level tech job market has changed, and new developers need to adapt. In the US, employment for software developers aged 22–25 has dropped nearly 20% since late 2022 (Stanford Digital Economy Lab). Most new hiring is going to experienced engineers, and juniors are now expected to do what mid-level engineers did a few years ago. But here’s the other side: talent is no longer limited by location. Remote work and freelance platforms mean a skilled developer anywhere can work with teams across the world. The traditional entry door is narrower, but the global one is wider than ever. From my own work in QA automation, one thing stands out: teams don’t just want people who can write code. They want people who can prove it works, find where it breaks, and keep it secure. That mindset is what’s pulling me toward cybersecurity. What this means for students and early-career developers: 🔹 Don’t wait for a job posting. Land your first paid project, even a small one, before you graduate. 🔹 Build one real, deployed project with users rather than ten tutorial apps. 🔹 Learn to work with AI tools, not around them. Interviews now test this. 🔹 Specialize: security, cloud, data, QA automation, or AI engineering. 🔹 Make your work visible on GitHub and LinkedIn. A degree opens the conversation. Proof of work closes it. To the experienced professionals in my network 👇 Looking back at your early career, what’s one piece of advice you wish someone had given you? A few words from you could make a real difference for someone just starting out. Students, what’s one thing you’re building this semester? #TechCareers #CyberSecurity #QAAutomation #SoftwareTesting #CareerAdvice

posts.author: mendel k
posts.headline: Talent Acquisition @ HireMe
posts.text: Bypass the long queue. Find junior tech jobs directly from hiring managers. New grads, career changers, interns: applying to job boards can feel like sending your resume into a black hole. Many entry-level tech roles get announced another way entirely. You can find them. Here's your LinkedIn search hack to uncover hidden opportunities: Go to LinkedIn and use the main search bar: Type: ("junior software engineer" OR "entry-level developer") AND "hiring" Then, apply these filters: 1. Click "Posts" at the top (not "People" or "Jobs"). 2. Refine by "Date posted" to "Past 24 hours" or "Past Week." Why this works: Many hiring managers don't wait for the official job board to post. They announce new roles, especially junior ones, directly in their LinkedIn feed. These posts often come from the actual team leads or directors who are building the team. This means you're seeing opportunities earlier, often before they hit crowded job sites. Fewer applicants, more direct visibility to the decision-maker. Engage thoughtfully with these posts. Show your interest. Or, if appropriate, send a direct, personalized connection request. HireMe also aggregates thousands of junior roles. This hack gives you a unique edge in finding your first tech job. Which junior tech role will you search for first with this hack? 🤔 #JuniorTech #JobSearchHack #LinkedInTips #NewGrad

posts.author: Aziz Shahhuseynov
posts.headline: Senior Fullstack Developer • Review Master • Your Favorite IT Mentor
posts.text: What started as a harmless joke on Twitter unexpectedly turned into a much larger conversation about the state of tech hiring. Yesterday, I joked that I might soon start responding to every job rejection by releasing an open-source alternative to the company’s SaaS product. Within several hours, the post reached over 100,000 impressions, 4,6k likes, and hundreds of reposts and comments, reaching an audience far beyond my usual network. But the numbers aren’t what I find most interesting. It’s the reaction behind them. I believe this reflects a growing frustration with how the tech industry approaches hiring. We live in a strange time when a company can spend months recruiting developers, put candidates through five rounds of interviews, assign technical assessments, and ultimately reject someone who may be perfectly capable of independently building a significant part of its product. Meanwhile, AI-assisted development is fundamentally changing the economics of software engineering. The cost of building software is decreasing. The time required to turn an idea into a working product is shrinking. And the gap between what an individual developer and an established engineering team can accomplish is becoming narrower. This raises an interesting question: What happens to an already dysfunctional hiring system when demonstrating your abilities by building a real product becomes easier than passing the interview process? Of course, writing code is not the same as building a successful business. Product-market fit, distribution, customer relationships, and operational execution remain significant challenges. But that’s not the point. Historically, established companies had a substantial advantage in engineering resources. Today, small teams, and increasingly individual developers, can achieve results that would have required entire departments just a few years ago. In my view, this shift could eventually force companies to reconsider how they evaluate technical talent. Perhaps AI won’t just transform how software is developed. It may also challenge the traditional relationship between employers and developers. And judging by the response to what was originally just a joke, this conversation is long overdue. Could the next wave of open source be driven not only by collaboration and innovation, but also by developers pushing back against the way the industry hires talent?

posts.text: Your resume might not be the problem. Your job search strategy might be. I came across a post on X from a software engineer who had resigned two months ago. Zero interview calls. Zero responses. And no clarity on whether the problem was his resume, skills, or the job market. Looking at his profile, one thing stood out to me. He had worked as a Software Engineer Trainee and Apprentice. And here's the reality of the Indian job market that many early-career professionals don't understand. Companies don't always count trainee and apprenticeship experience the same way they count full-time professional experience. You may have worked on real projects. You may have built production systems. You may have developed valuable technical skills. But recruiters and hiring filters may still evaluate you as a fresher or entry-level candidate. So, what should you do? Here's my advice: - Target the right roles. Prioritize fresher positions and jobs asking for 0–1 or 0–2 years of experience. - Don't blindly apply to experienced roles. If a job requires 3+ years of professional experience, your application may struggle to pass the initial screening. - Showcase your actual work. Highlight production projects, measurable impact, technologies used, and problems you've solved. - Position your experience honestly. Make your trainee or apprenticeship designation clear, while demonstrating the skills you've developed. - Don't assume the market has no jobs. First, check whether you're targeting the right roles and presenting your profile effectively. One important caveat: some companies do count apprenticeships and trainee experience. It depends on the employer, role, and nature of the work. The goal isn't to make your experience look smaller. It's to make your profile relevant to the jobs you're targeting. Sometimes, a better-targeted job search can make a bigger difference than sending out another 100 applications.

posts.text: Same job. Same title. Different postcode. A software engineer in India starts at a median of $15K in total compensation. In the US, the same engineer starts at $141K. That is 9.2x. By senior level the gap narrows to 4.8x, $52K against $251K. It is still huge, but it was widest on day one. Even the top 10 percent of entry level engineers in India earn $33K. That is less than a quarter of the US median of $141K. - Entry level, median: $15K in India, $141K in the US (9.2x) - Entry level, top 10%: $33K, $223K (6.7x) - Senior, median: $52K, $251K (4.8x) - Senior, top 10%: $107K, $495K (4.6x) If you are starting out, this is the strongest case I know for looking at remote roles with companies outside India from the very first job, not the fifth. Numbers are self-reported, 2,329 entry level reports in India and 6,792 in the US, and before cost of living. 💬 Did your first job pay what you expected? What would you tell a fresher today? 🔗 If you're looking for your next role, startups hiring are on NextDoor.Company

posts.text: If every IT company wants experienced developers, who will create the next generation of experienced developers? Something I have been thinking about lately. With AI changing the software industry, many students are becoming hesitant to choose software development as a career. At the same time, companies continue to look for experienced developers who can contribute from day one. But every experienced developer was once a fresher. Someone gave them their first opportunity. Someone trusted them with their first project. Someone helped them learn beyond textbooks. As a founder of Quoretex Technologies, we are trying to do our part by hiring freshers, training them, and giving them opportunities to contribute to real-world software projects. But smaller IT companies cannot create enough opportunities alone. The industry needs a broader approach. Here is one practical idea for large and mid-sized IT companies: Instead of assigning every small initiative to internal teams, consider partnering with emerging IT companies for: • Small, well-defined software development projects • Proof of concepts (PoCs) and pilot initiatives • Internal automation tools and workflow improvements • Module development, testing, and maintenance • Non-critical enhancements to existing applications With clear requirements, appropriate supervision, and quality standards, these engagements can create value for both sides. The enterprise gets an opportunity to evaluate a new delivery partner with manageable risk. The smaller IT company gets the opportunity to build its capabilities, deliver meaningful work, and train freshers on real business problems. And the next generation of developers gets something that no course or AI tool can fully replace: practical experience, accountability, and the opportunity to learn by building. AI will continue to change how software is developed. We should embrace it and teach young developers to use it responsibly. But let's not allow the transition to an AI-driven industry to close the entry-level door for the very people who will build its future. My request to enterprise leaders, CTOs, delivery heads, and procurement teams: Consider giving emerging IT companies a chance to deliver small projects. You might discover a capable long-term technology partner while helping develop the next generation of engineering talent. At Quoretex Technologies, we are committed to building that talent and delivering real-world software solutions from Amravati, Maharashtra. Let's build the next generation of developers, not just search for the existing one. What do you think? Can small, structured project engagements help bridge the gap between freshers and industry expectations? #SoftwareDevelopment #FutureOfWork #AI #Freshers #ITServices #TalentDevelopment #QuoretexTechnologies

posts.author: Ritik Singh
posts.headline: Building AI Agents & SaaS Products | Agentic AI & Workflow Automation | Building in Public
posts.text: Are we watching an AI bubble or are some people living in a bubble about what AI can already do? “AI will disappear when the hype dies.” Before saying that, ask a founder: How many junior developers are you hiring? How much routine design work are you outsourcing? How many people do you need for first-line support? Which vacancies are you choosing not to refill? Those answers matter as much as the layoff headlines. AI doesn’t have to replace an entire profession to change its economics. It can take over enough tasks that a business changes its next hiring decision. 1. SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT Implementation, tests, documentation, coding and debugging are all areas where teams are already using AI. The question is whether the same team can deliver more and whether that changes how many additional developers it hires. Junior developers also need those tasks to learn. What replaces that training ground? 2. DESIGN AND CREATIVE WORK AI-assisted work extends beyond basic social posts: image editing, compositing, campaign concepts, and creative variations. Advanced design still needs taste, consistency, usability, and direction. But if production becomes faster, clients may change what they’re willing to pay for and teams may change who they hire. 3. BPO AND CUSTOMER SUPPORT Voice agents can be configured to answer routine questions, manage bookings, and route requests. Human support remains essential for difficult cases. Still, moving routine calls to software can change staffing, training, and the economics of outsourced support. 4. CONTENT AND BACK-OFFICE WORK First drafts. Transcription. Document extraction. Data entry. Routine reporting. For work built around repeatable outputs, “AI isn’t perfect” is an incomplete response. The business comparison includes human errors, review costs, and the quality required for that particular task. There is an early hiring signal, too. Stanford and ADP’s August 2026 research found a roughly 19% employment shortfall for US workers aged 22–25 in highly AI-exposed occupations, relative to less-exposed peers. The researchers found no widespread economy-wide displacement and did not establish that AI caused the gap. The adjustment appeared mainly through reduced hiring. That deserves attention not a victory lap. Some AI companies may be overvalued. Some products may fail. Useful capabilities can survive both. My bet: we’re early in the redesign of work. The effects will differ by role, company, and country. If you hire developers, designers, or support staff: Has AI changed the number or the experience level of people you plan to hire? #AI #FutureOfWork #AIAgents #SoftwareEngineering

posts.text: Our hiring post in September was our most-seen post of the last three months. So here's something useful for everyone who's applying for their first tech job. 👇 5 things that make a fresher resume easy to shortlist: 1️⃣ Lead with the role and your stack. One line at the top: "Junior Software Developer · Java · SQL · React". The top of the page gets read first. 2️⃣ Show 2–3 projects, not 10. For each one: the problem it solved, what you built yourself, and a link. 3️⃣ Make your GitHub readable. A README with setup steps and a screenshot beats 40 empty repositories. 4️⃣ List only skills you can explain. If it's on your resume, expect a question on it. 5️⃣ Keep it to one clean page. Save it as a PDF named FirstName_LastName_Resume.pdf. Freshers and final-year students: what's the one thing you're unsure about on your resume? Ask in the comments and our team will reply. posts.text: 🚨 "We're hiring a DevOps Engineer." A few weeks later... They're expected to build an Internal Developer Platform, manage Kubernetes, write Terraform, set up CI/CD, respond to production incidents, improve developer experience, and ensure reliability. Sound familiar? The truth is: 👉 DevOps is a culture. 👉 Platform Engineering is a product. 👉 SRE is an engineering discipline. They're not competing—they're solving different parts of the same problem. Think of it like building a highway: 🛣️ Platform Engineering builds the road. Self-service platforms, golden paths, and developer experience. ⚙️ DevOps keeps the traffic moving. Automation, CI/CD, Infrastructure as Code, and faster software delivery. 🛡️ SRE ensures the bridge never collapses. SLOs, observability, incident response, and reliability at scale. The strongest engineering organizations don't choose one over the other. They combine all three to deliver software that's fast, reliable, and easy to ship. The real challenge isn't deciding between Platform Engineering, DevOps, or SRE. It's knowing when each discipline adds the most value. 💬 What's your take? posts.text: Why ?? #React Jobs Are #Reducing (and What I’m Doing About It) When I searched on multiple platforms ( #Naukri, #LinkedIn, #Indeed, #CutShort), I noticed that pure “React Developer” roles are fewer compared to previous years. After speaking with several people in the industry and checking job trends, here’s what I understood: 🔹 Companies are no longer hiring React-only roles. 🔹 The titles changed to broader roles like Frontend Engineer, UI Developer, Product Engineer Frontend, Software Engineer UI, etc. 🔹 Most companies now expect React + TypeScript + Next.js + APIs instead of just React. 🔹 Modern frontend roles demand stronger fundamentals in JavaScript, HTML, CSS, REST, GraphQL, state management, and UI performance. 🔹 The market is crowded with many juniors who learned only React basics, so hiring is more selective now. React is NOT dying — but React-only jobs are reducing. 𝗜 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗱 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄 𝗣𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗮𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗚𝘂𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗙𝗿𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝗱 𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗿𝘀. covering JavaScript, React, Next.js, System Design, and more. posts.author: Priyanka Khandelwal
posts.headline: Co-Founder at Emper.ai
posts.text: What if insurance wasn’t something Employees struggled to understand, but something that genuinely helped them make better decisions for their lives? That’s the idea behind Emper.ai We’re building an AI-powered personal insurance platform for corporate employees, bringing together AI and human expertise to make insurance simpler, more personalized, and easier to navigate from understanding coverage to making informed decisions as life evolves. And we’re just getting started! To bring this vision to life, we’re looking for a Full-Stack Engineer (SDE II) - AI Applications who loves building from the ground up, enjoys solving complex problems, and is excited about putting AI to work on real-world challenges. What will you build at Emper.ai? 1)AI-powered experiences: Build intelligent applications using LLMs, prompt engineering, structured outputs, and guardrails. 2)Smarter information retrieval: Design RAG pipelines, embeddings, vector search, and hybrid retrieval systems. 3)End-to-end products: Own features across modern frontend frameworks, backend APIs, and AI services. 4)Scalable engineering: Build event-driven services, robust data layers, and reliable application architecture. 5)AI you can trust - Help us build secure, privacy-conscious applications with meaningful evaluation and observability. But building great products is only half the story. We believe great work happens when people have the freedom to think differently, speak openly, experiment boldly, and enjoy the journey together. At Emper, that means: Play hard, work smart: Monthly sporting events and a little friendly competition! Friday Funday: Lunch, laughter, and great company. On us! Think. Speak. Challenge: Your ideas matter. Your voice counts. Who should apply? Someone with 3+ years of production software engineering experience, solid full-stack skills, hands-on experience building LLM/GenAI applications and RAG systems, and most importantly the curiosity and willingness to turn ideas into products people love using. You don't just want to write code. You want to build, experiment, challenge assumptions, and see your work make a difference. 📍 Mumbai | Full-time | Product Engineering At Emper.ai, you’ll have the opportunity to shape an early-stage product, influence engineering decisions, and help build an AI-first platform in a space that touches millions of working Indians. If building at the intersection of AI, technology, and real human needs excites you, let's talk. Let's build something that matters. DM me to explore the opportunity or tag someone in your network who should be part of this journey. #Hiring #EmperAI #GenAI #FullStackEngineer #AIEngineering #LLM #RAG #StartupJobs #MumbaiJobs

posts.author: IMT Resourcing Solutions
posts.text: The tech salary landscape in Bristol is shifting, and it isn’t just about numbers anymore. In the South West, demand for MSP engineers, software developers, and cyber security specialists remains elevated, but hiring budgets are tightening and expectations are evolving. Companies are balancing higher base salaries with improved benefits, more flexible working patterns, and clearer pathways to leadership roles. For candidates, it’s about value beyond salary: challenging projects, modern tech stacks, and visible impact on customer outcomes. A few practical signals I’m seeing right now: - Practical career ladders matter more than lofty title changes. Teams investing in upskilling see better retention than those chasing rapid promotion cycles. - Strong, policy-driven remote/hybrid options attract candidates who would otherwise go elsewhere, particularly for senior IT roles. - Companies offering structured onboarding and mentorship for junior to mid-level roles are winning in the long game, even if initial salaries aren’t the highest. If you’re hiring in Bristol or the wider South West, align incentives with real-day impact: clear project milestones, peer learning, and a transparent path to leadership. For candidates, map not just salary but growth, learning, and impact. What growth priorities are shaping your tech teams this quarter in the South West? Are you seeing the same balance between salary and development opportunities? #SouthWestUK #TechRecruitment #BristolTech #HiringTrends #CyberSecurity #MSP #SoftwareDevelopment #ITSupport

posts.author: Ihar Vakulski
posts.headline: Driving SaaS Growth with Data & CRO | Founder @ SaaSFunnelLab
posts.text: I think the value of being able to write code is decreasing every month. More people can now build software with Claude, ChatGPT, and other AI tools. Something that previously required hiring a developer is becoming something you can try building yourself. I’m already hearing about entrepreneurs creating tools for their own businesses instead of paying another monthly subscription. This isn’t happening at a huge scale yet. But it has started, and I expect it to grow. For software companies, that means your competition can include a customer deciding, “I could build what I need myself”. That’s a much bigger problem than another competitor adding your best feature. If almost anyone can build a tool, buying software starts to feel like buying cucumbers at the supermarket. Plenty to choose from, and most look pretty similar. And that’s why I believe marketing and distribution are becoming more important than coding today. Who knows you exist? Why do they remember you? Why would they trust your product enough to pay for it when there are ten or hundreds alternatives, including building something themselves? You need convincing answers. I work in marketing, so yes, I have a strong opinion here. If I were starting a software business today, I’d worry much more about reaching customers and earning their trust than how quickly I could ship. I can use AI to help me build a product. I can’t assume anyone will care that I did.

posts.headline: UX, HCI Research and Design Engineer | Former Web Intern @Michigan Medicine | MSI (HCI) @University of Michigan, Ann Arbor
posts.text: I made a Self Positioning Canvas about myself. So I thought, why not finally write my intro for LinkedIn. I am currently completing my master's degree in Information (specializing in UX Research and Design) at the University of Michigan's School of Information. Previously, I had been a computer science engineer student experimenting with programming technologies. Then, my curiosity shifted from the technology itself to the people using it. Exciting stuff I've done since coming to UMSI: 🔹 Worked on some really cool healthcare and software-based UX projects in different kinds of roles, and now currently on my Mastery Project as the sole product manager, researcher and designer. 🔹 Interned at Michigan Medicine as a part of the Web Team for the Department of Communications. 🔹 Prototyping in Figma Make, Claude Code, and ChatGPT, because “wouldn’t it be cool if...” is my favorite sentence. 🔹 Learned about Usability Testing, Needs Assessment, Visual Communication, Interaction Design and Product Management over the course of 3 semesters. Outside of school, I love to make crochet projects and play with different coffee recipes. Turns out looping yarn and brewing the perfect coffee drink all train the same muscle: paying very close attention. Here is where I ask for something. I graduate in December 2026 and I’m looking for Associate PM, entry-level PM, and UX research roles in health tech, software and AI-enabled products. I’m happiest where research, data, and engineering all end up in the same room (and actually talk to each other). If your team is hiring, or you know someone who should meet me, my inbox is open and my portfolio is here: styarla.github.io Thanks for reading. Better late than never, right? #UXResearch #ProductManagement #HealthTech #UMSI

posts.author: Mira Ling
posts.headline: Co-Founder & CPO @ Ambitology.com | Building career and opening for a tech job?
posts.text: AI job titles are multiplying—and that can make it harder to see where you fit. A recent r/developersIndia discussion came from a 2026 graduate weighing SDE-1 and forward-deployed roles after experience across software, full stack, product, and ML research. The Friday thread had 19 upvotes and 13 comments when I checked. A newer Sunday question from a Python full-stack developer choosing between GenAI Engineer, ML Engineer, and other paths had 2 votes and 3 comments. Those are community conversations, not proof of hiring demand. You don’t need to choose your whole future based on a title. Start with the work: • Find the problems a role asks you to solve. • Pick one project that shows relevant skills in action. • Be ready to explain what you built, how you checked it, and what you’d improve. A title can point you toward a door; your work shows what you bring through it. As a founder, I believe career decisions get clearer when you can see how your skills connect to possible next roles. Ambitology Skill Graph helps connect learning and skills with roles that may fit. https://lnkd.in/g4wUvBUB If you’re exploring AI work, which role family feels closest to your strengths?

posts.text: Robots are about to work next to millions of people. Somebody has to write the code that keeps them safe. 🤖🛡️ Our Compass team at Amazon Robotics is growing, and we're hiring software engineers in Pasadena, CA. Compass is building the certified safety foundation for Amazon's entire robotics fleet. We work alongside the inventors of control barrier functions on a universal approach to safe autonomy. It has to work across mobile robots, manipulators, mobile manipulators, and even legged and dynamically stable platforms. The goal: safety that never gets in the way of performance. We have two kinds of engineering roles open: ⚙️ Embedded Robotics SDE Take algorithms from our R&D team and turn them into production-grade, certifiable embedded software (think C++, MISRA/AUTOSAR-style standards, deterministic real-time execution). You'll own the library of safety-critical modules and carry it through the full certification lifecycle, from research prototype to certified product. 🔗 Robotics SDE, Safe Autonomy Own how Compass plugs into real robots. You'll design the abstractions and APIs that separate safety logic from hardware, connect with motion planning, perception, and safety-rated firmware, and build the simulation pipelines that prove it all works, at fleet scale. Both are open at the mid and senior levels. You might be a great fit if you: ✔️ Write C++ (or Rust) for real-time or embedded systems ✔️ Care about reliability, traceability, and doing things the right way ✔️ Enjoy working with research-minded teams on hard, unsolved problems ✔️ Want your code to sit between a robot and the people around it Bonus points for experience with ROS/ROS2, functional safety standards, control barrier functions, RTOS, or robot simulation. posts.text: Just hit 2,000 internship applications over three years. Freshman year me just spammed generic resumes and hoped for the best. Fast forward to now, and it turns out most standard advice is just pretty mid. Narrowing down 2,000 applications to three real takeaways: 𝟏. 𝐁𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐝 𝐚 𝐝𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐲 𝐡𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐭 𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝐰𝐚𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐫𝐞𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐫𝐚𝐥𝐬. Waiting weeks for a referral usually means missing the review cap entirely. Checking daily boards and submitting within the first 24 hours lands your resume right at the top of the stack. 𝟐. 𝐈𝐧𝐟𝐨 𝐬𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐥𝐨𝐰-𝐤𝐞𝐲 𝐧𝐚𝐦𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐠𝐧𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐡𝐮𝐛𝐬. Show up, ask sharp questions, and get your resume onto internal event lists. Recruiters remember engaged faces, and they usually share direct hiring timelines or direct consideration links before the public rush. 𝟑. 𝐌𝐚𝐤𝐞 𝐲𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐞𝐧𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐣𝐮𝐝𝐠𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐨𝐛𝐯𝐢𝐨𝐮𝐬 𝐨𝐧𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞. Recruiters started reaching out directly once I stopped relying just on cold applications. Posting my hackathon projects on LinkedIn, breaking down my work, and having a personal website to show demos makes it clear what I can actually build. Mass applying gives you baseline reps, but personal branding is what actually gets eyes on your work. #swe #internships #wagmi

posts.text: Software Developer Job Postings Rise Despite AI Coding Automation. AI Can Write Code, But It Still Needs Adult Supervision. The Structural Shift in Tech Hiring: Seniority and AI Systems Engineering. Why AI is Driving Demand for Senior Developers. Software developers were supposed to be first in line for the AI guillotine. Yet, despite artificial intelligence now writing a third of all new code and automating routine programming tasks, US software developer job postings have ironically climbed nearly 15 percent since early 2025. The controversy is stark: the machines have not replaced the engineering department, they have simply redefined what an engineer actually does. This trend is a vital signal for chief technology officers, tech recruiters, and computer science graduates. As generative AI turns code generation into a cheap commodity, the market is aggressively rewarding developers who can review, integrate, and architect systems, proving that verifying code is now far more valuable than writing it. The current hiring rebound is highly concentrated. Employment data reveals that 71 percent of the recent increase in developer postings comes from senior roles, with a significant chunk explicitly requiring AI expertise. While overall postings remain below pre pandemic peaks, the demand for experienced talent is surging. Writing code is no longer the bottleneck for software teams. The new constraint is systems judgment. Companies are desperate for experienced architects who can oversee AI agents, wire generated code into complex legacy systems, and take accountability for the final product when the algorithm inevitably makes a mistake. Meanwhile, the entry level pipeline is collapsing. Hiring for early career software developers has plunged by roughly 20 percent since the generative AI boom began. The foundational junior tasks that historically served as a training ground for new graduates have been almost entirely automated. This creates a ticking time bomb for the tech industry. If companies refuse to hire and train junior developers today because an AI can do the basic work cheaper, they are virtually guaranteeing a catastrophic shortage of the very senior engineers they so desperately need a few years from now. posts.text: Google opened 130 new senior-and-above US engineering roles last week. Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Apple, Oracle, NVIDIA, and Netflix together posted 927 new core roles. They also closed 1,077. I track this every Monday now. The closes still outpace the opens. The market isn't hiring like 2021. It's swapping seats. Roles disappear, new ones show up with AI in the title, and a lot of senior people are stuck wondering where they fit. 334 of the 1,806 new US engineering roles I tracked this week were AI/ML. About 18%. Here's the part that surprised me. The median senior AI/ML base now starts at $174,000. Senior SWE starts at $168,100. At the top of the band, AI/ML is about $17K higher. So "learn AI" isn't a raise by itself. Landing higher in the band is. I spent years at Amazon, Microsoft, and Oracle, most recently as a Principal engineer, and I sat in a lot of loops. The people who cleared the top of the band weren't always the ones with the flashiest stack. They could explain what they owned, the tradeoffs they made, and why it mattered to the business. That's a skill. It can be practiced. If you're a senior engineer looking at one of these Big Tech or AI roles and you're not sure where you'd land, DM me "fit check." I'll tell you honestly whether coaching makes sense, and if it doesn't, I'll say so. (Postings show base pay only, not stock or bonus.)

posts.author: Alessandro Furlanetto
posts.headline: Technical Lead & Architect | AI‑Augmented SDLC | DevSecOps & Governance | Identity & Distributed Systems
posts.text: AI is killing junior software jobs. That's the narrative I've been hearing for months. Then I looked at the facts. Yes, employment among younger software developers in the US is below the 2022 peak. That's a signal worth watching carefully. But a 20% decline in hiring is not the same thing as the extinction of a profession. If companies hired 100 junior developers before and now hire 80, that's a market adjustment. Not a collapse. What I find particularly interesting is that Accenture, one of the world's most aggressive adopters and sellers of AI solutions, publicly stated that it plans to hire more entry-level talent in 2026 than it did in 2025. That's a curious strategy for a company that should, theoretically, understand AI-driven workforce disruption before most others. Perhaps we're looking at the wrong variable. We often describe a senior engineer as a junior engineer with more years of coding experience. I'm not convinced; a senior professional is not the person who remembers the most APIs, frameworks, or commands. A senior professional understands context. They: - identify the real problem. - navigate trade-offs. - make decisions under uncertainty. - own the consequences. AI is undoubtedly reducing the value of a great deal of routine technical work. What remains unproven is the assumption that routine technical work was the same thing as professional growth. Maybe AI isn't eliminating the path to expertise. Maybe it's eliminating some of the tasks we mistakenly confused with expertise. The real question isn't: "Who will do the work of junior developers?" The real question is: "How do we develop professional judgment in a world where execution is becoming almost free?" That is a much harder question. And probably the more important one. #AI #ArtificialIntelligence #SoftwareEngineering #Technology #Innovation #FutureOfWork #DigitalTransformation #Leadership #GenerativeAI #Accenture #TechLeadership #EngineeringManagement #RAndD #ProductDevelopment #TechTrends

posts.author: Joshua Reed
posts.headline: AI Infrastructure Engineer -- Member of Technical Staff at Andromeda
posts.text: I'm hiring, and so is the rest of Andromeda! Demand for AI compute is growing faster than any handful of providers can build. The GPUs exist, but they're scattered across hyperscalers, neoclouds and independent data centers, and they're hard to get when you need them. Andromeda is building the platform that makes all of that compute work as one, so model builders, research labs and inference teams get capacity when they need it. We want every spare electron doing useful work for AI. I'm leading the Platform team, and I'm growing the team by another 3-4 engineers, junior and senior. Platform is the part that makes it real. We turn racks of GPUs from anywhere into production-ready clusters with no human in the loop, then keep them healthy as they move from customer to customer. It's a hard systems problem, and it's at the center of the biggest infrastructure buildout of our lifetime. What I care about most is drive. I want people who chase a bug through four layers of the stack because they need to know why. People who own the outcome, not just the ticket, and who ship and then make it better. Skills can be taught. Hunger can't. If you've got that dog in you, I want to talk.
